Name: causal_asymmetry_probing
Title: Does It Know Which Way the Arrow Points? Probing Scientific Foundation Models for Encoded Causal Asymmetry
Short Hypothesis: Genuine scientific understanding requires representing the *direction* of a mechanism: temperature causes reaction-rate change (not vice versa), a destabilizing mutation causes lowered melting temperature (not the reverse), and CO2 concentration drives absorbance (not the reverse). A model that merely fits correlations will encode the *joint* co-variation of two coupled variables symmetrically, whereas a model with mechanistic understanding will encode the causal driver and the caused effect with a measurable representational asymmetry: intervening on / reading the cause should predict the effect far better than the reverse, and the two roles should occupy geometrically distinguishable subspaces. We hypothesize this causal-direction asymmetry is present for some scientific relationships and absent for others, providing a sharp diagnostic of mechanistic versus correlational encoding.
Related Work: Recent work shows scientific foundation models encode steerable concept directions: Physics Steering (Fear et al. 2025) injects delta-direction concepts to control physics simulations; Aurora atmospheric-chemistry probing (Hu et al. 2026) shows a first-order but non-mechanistic ozone response; SAE reviews (Orlov et al. 2026) flag annotation circularity; VLA steering (Häon et al. 2025) finds causal action directions. All of these test whether a *concept* is present and steerable, or whether outputs match known physics. None test whether the model encodes the *causal direction* (asymmetry) of a relationship between two coupled scientific variables. Causal-discovery foundation models (CausalMoE, Causal-KAN) learn causal graphs from data as an external task, but do not ask whether a *pretrained* scientific FM's internal geometry already distinguishes cause from effect. Our contribution is a novel, read-and-intervene asymmetry test: distinguishing directional mechanistic encoding from symmetric correlational encoding, applicable across domains, and orthogonal to all my prior proposals (which target laws, exponents, universality, superseded theories, conservation, ontology geometry, and validity domains) since none address causal-arrow directionality.
Abstract: A defining feature of scientific understanding is knowing which way a causal arrow points: raising temperature accelerates a reaction (not the reverse), a core-destabilizing mutation lowers a protein's melting temperature (not the reverse), and increasing a chromophore's concentration raises absorbance (not the reverse). A model that only fits correlations sees two coupled variables symmetrically; a model with mechanistic understanding should encode the cause and the effect asymmetrically. We introduce Causal-Asymmetry Probing, a framework that tests whether scientific foundation models internally distinguish causes from effects. For each of ~10 mechanisms with a known cause->effect direction across chemistry, biology, physics, and materials, we (1) locate representational directions for the cause variable and the effect variable via linear probes, and (2) run two complementary asymmetry tests: an interventional test (steering the cause direction should shift the model's prediction of the effect more than steering the effect direction shifts its prediction of the cause) and a geometric/predictive test (the cause subspace should predict the effect variable better than the effect subspace predicts the cause, beyond what symmetric mutual information allows). We define a Causal-Asymmetry Score aggregating interventional and predictive asymmetry, benchmarked against a symmetric-null (variable pairs with no causal direction, e.g., two co-varying descriptors) and a randomly-initialized-model control. Applied to open protein (ESM-2), molecular (ChemBERTa/MolFormer), and physics/atmospheric models, the framework yields a cheap, reproducible audit of whether a scientific model knows which way its arrows point.
Experiments: 1. Mechanism curation (~10 directed pairs with a known cause->effect arrow and an experimental/simulated dataset providing counterfactual ground truth): chemistry/physics -- temperature -> reaction rate (Arrhenius datasets), chromophore concentration -> absorbance (Beer-Lambert), pressure -> volume (gas datasets), reactive-nitrogen emission -> ozone (atmospheric reanalysis, following Aurora); biology -- core-destabilizing mutation -> melting temperature (MegaScale/FireProtDB ddG deep mutational scans), GC content / codon usage -> mRNA stability; materials -- composition/electronegativity -> bandgap (Materials Project). 2. Symmetric-null pairs: pairs of variables that co-vary but have no direct causal arrow between them (e.g., two collinear molecular descriptors, or two properties both driven by a hidden common cause), used to calibrate what 'no asymmetry' looks like. 3. Models: ESM-2 (8M-650M) for protein pairs, ChemBERTa/MolFormer for molecular pairs, and a public physics/atmospheric FM (e.g., an open weather/continuum emulator) for physics pairs; extract token/pooled representations at all layers. 4. Direction localization: fit linear probes to read each variable (cause and effect) from representations; pick best-layer directions and record probe R^2. 5. Interventional asymmetry test: perform activation steering along the cause direction and measure the induced change in the model's predicted effect (delta_effect|cause); then steer along the effect direction and measure induced change in predicted cause (delta_cause|effect). Compute interventional asymmetry A_int = (|delta_effect|cause| - |delta_cause|effect|) normalized by their sum; a mechanistic model should give A_int > 0 (steering the cause moves the effect more). Cross-validate with activation patching from real paired inputs differing only in the cause. 6. Predictive/geometric asymmetry test: measure how well the cause subspace linearly predicts the effect variable vs. how well the effect subspace predicts the cause, reporting the difference beyond the symmetric baseline (mutual-information / bidirectional-regression control), and measure subspace separability (cosine/CKA between cause and effect directions). 7. Causal-Asymmetry Score (CAS): combine A_int and predictive-asymmetry, per pair and layer. 8. Validation against ground truth: for pairs with counterfactual data (DMS ddG, atmospheric perturbations), test whether the interventional asymmetry magnitude tracks the true causal effect asymmetry; test whether CAS is high for directed pairs and near-zero for symmetric-null pairs (report AUROC of CAS distinguishing directed from null pairs). 9. Controls: randomly-initialized-model null, random-direction steering null, and off-manifold checks (patching from real inputs). 10. Scaling analysis: track CAS across model sizes to test whether directional understanding emerges with scale. Metrics: A_int, predictive asymmetry, subspace separability, CAS, CAS-vs-ground-truth correlation, and directed-vs-null AUROC. Deliverable: an open directed-mechanism benchmark and per-model Causal-Asymmetry leaderboard.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Interventional asymmetry could arise from tokenization or representational-scale differences between the two variables rather than true causal structure; we mitigate with the symmetric-null pairs (matched co-varying, non-directed) and by normalizing steering magnitude in probe-standardized units. 2. Activation steering can push off-manifold, producing artifactual asymmetries; we cross-validate with activation patching from real paired inputs and off-manifold detection. 3. For some coupled variables the true causal direction is debated or bidirectional; we restrict to pairs with textbook-clear arrows and report ambiguous pairs separately. 4. Predictive asymmetry can be confounded when one variable is intrinsically easier to decode (higher SNR) regardless of causality; the symmetric-null control and interventional test triangulate against this. 5. Linear probes may miss nonlinearly encoded variables; we add nonlinear-probe robustness checks and treat linear results as a lower bound. 6. Counterfactual ground truth for asymmetry is richest in biology (DMS) and atmospheric (perturbation) settings and sparser elsewhere, restricting some pairs to interventional-only or geometric-only tests. 7. Findings are pair- and model-specific, but this diagnostic specificity is the intended output, and the ground-truth validation makes the asymmetry signal actionable rather than purely descriptive.
